market_context: United States; imported Spanish Iberian ham and Spanish legal labeling
title: What do the black, red, green and white labels on Iberian ham mean?

seo.title: What do the colors on Iberian ham labels mean?
seo.meta_description: Black = acorn-fed 100% Iberian; red = acorn-fed Iberian; green = field-fed Iberian; white = feed-fed Iberian. Spain's official seal colors identify production category.
seo.search_intent: Help U.S. buyers understand Spain's black, red, green and white seals on Iberian ham and what each category actually guarantees.

excerpt: Spain's Iberian-ham seal colors are legally defined. Black means acorn-fed 100% Iberian; red means acorn-fed Iberian; green means field-fed Iberian; white means feed-fed Iberian. Only black guarantees 100% Iberian genetics from the color alone. On red, green and white products, read the label for the Iberian breed percentage.
content_html:
The black, red, green and white seals on Spanish Iberian ham are not marketing colors chosen independently by producers. They are defined by Spain's Iberian quality standard to identify production categories.

The four official colors

SealSpanish categoryMeaning
BlackDe bellota 100% ibéricoAcorn-fed + 100% Iberian breed
RedDe bellota ibéricoAcorn-fed + Iberian cross
GreenDe cebo de campo ibéricoField-feed production category
WhiteDe cebo ibéricoFeed-based production category

Spain's Royal Decree 4/2014 requires hams and shoulders to carry an inviolable color-coded seal with a unique individual number.

Black: acorn-fed and 100% Iberian

The black seal is the only color that tells you both feeding category and full breed purity: de bellota 100% ibérico. The protected phrase pata negra is reserved for this designation.

Red: still acorn-fed, but not 100%

Red means de bellota ibérico. The pig met the acorn-fed production requirements, but it was not 100% Iberian.

The breed percentage must be stated on the label when the animal is not 100% Iberian, commonly 50% or 75% Iberian.

Green and white describe feeding systems

Green identifies cebo de campo ibérico; white identifies cebo ibérico. Neither color by itself tells you the exact breed percentage, so read the full label.

A green or white product can therefore have different Iberian breed percentages depending on its genetics.

How to read the seal together with the rest of the label

The colored seal is best treated as the first line of information, not the entire description. After identifying the color, read the sales designation for the feeding category and the stated Iberian breed percentage. A red seal, for example, tells you the product is acorn-fed Iberian ham, while the rest of the labeling tells you whether the animal was 50% or 75% Iberian. Green and white seals likewise need the breed statement beside them. That two-step reading prevents the common mistake of assuming every product marked “Ibérico” has the same genetics.

The seal also does not encode curing time. Two hams with the same legal category can spend different periods maturing and can come from legs of different sizes. Salt penetration, fat distribution, cellar conditions and the producer's process all influence aroma and texture after the legal production category has already been established. That is why two products carrying the same color can taste noticeably different and command very different prices without either one having an incorrect seal.

It helps to distinguish the official seal from the decorative band, box or brand colors added later. Premium packaging can use black, red or gold graphics for marketing, but the regulated color coding refers to the numbered seal attached to the ham or shoulder. When buying a whole piece, look for that physical identifier rather than inferring category from the presentation. With sliced packaged ham, the complete legal name and breed percentage on the label become especially important because the original seal is not in front of you.

The words “bellota” and “100% Ibérico” answer different questions. Bellota describes the top feeding and finishing category under the standard, while 100% Ibérico describes breed purity. Black combines both conditions. Red keeps the bellota production category but allows crossbred animals that meet the required Iberian percentage. This is why a simple hierarchy based only on color can be misleading: the colors bundle several production variables rather than representing a laboratory score for flavor or nutrition.

For comparison shopping, use the seal to verify the production claim first, then compare breed percentage, producer, weight, curing information and price within that category. A black-seal ham is legally a very specific product, but the seal cannot promise that every diner will prefer its flavor to every red-seal ham. Personal preference still depends on saltiness, fat character, maturation and slicing. The regulatory system tells you what the product is; tasting tells you which one you like.

If you are buying outside Spain, translated marketing language may simplify the legal Spanish designation. Whenever possible, look for the original category wording and the breed percentage instead of relying on phrases such as “premium Iberian” alone. Those phrases may be descriptive, but they are not a substitute for the regulated information that separates bellota, cebo de campo and cebo categories.

The seal is not a four-level tasting score

Color identifies the legal production category. Within the same category, curing time, producer, salt, fat infiltration and sensory quality can still differ substantially.

Use the color to understand the production claim, not as a complete prediction of how good the ham will taste.

faq.question: Which seal is 100% Iberian acorn-fed ham?
faq.answer: Black. It identifies de bellota 100% ibérico and is the category allowed to use the protected term pata negra.

faq.question: Is the red seal also acorn-fed?
faq.answer: Yes. Red is de bellota ibérico, but the pig is not 100% Iberian; check the label for breed percentage.

faq.question: Does green mean 100% Iberian?
faq.answer: No. Green identifies the cebo de campo production category. Breed percentage is separate information.
